**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The first word is always the hardest. It sits on the tip of your tongue, heavy with possibility, trembling with the weight of what comes next. A thousand words—how much can they hold? A lifetime? A single breath? The answer is both and neither. Words are fragile things, easily broken, easily misinterpreted, easily forgotten. But when strung together, they become something more. They become a bridge, a weapon, a confession, a lie.

I once knew a man who collected words like other people collect stamps. He kept them in jars, on scraps of paper, in the margins of books. He said words were alive, that they shifted meaning depending on who spoke them, when they were spoken, how they were spoken. He believed in the power of the unsaid as much as the spoken. "Silence is a word too," he told me once, "the most powerful one of all."

I didn’t understand then. I do now.

Words have carried me through storms and left me stranded in calm seas. They’ve built me up and torn me down. They’ve been my armor and my undoing. A thousand words—what could they possibly mean? Everything. Nothing. It depends on who’s reading them.

I write this not because I have something to say, but because I have something to un-say. To undo. To erase. Words are ghosts. They linger long after the speaker is gone. They haunt the pages, the air, the spaces between people. They shape the world, one syllable at a time.

And so, I write. Not because I must, but because I can. Because the weight of a thousand words is lighter than the weight of silence. Because sometimes, the only way to carry the truth is to let it spill out, unfiltered, unpolished, unapologetic.

A thousand words. That’s all I have. That’s all anyone has. What will you do with yours?
